items.title: You cannot reach absolute zero — and even there, atoms wiggle
items.claim: Absolute zero is 0 K, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The third law of thermodynamics says it's unattainable in finite steps. And even if you got there, atoms wouldn't stop moving.
items.prompt: Why can't atoms stop moving at 0 K?

options.text: Imperfect measurement makes them seem to move

Heisenberg uncertainty — atoms with zero kinetic energy would have zero momentum, but a perfectly known momentum implies infinite position uncertainty; the lowest-energy quantum state has irreducible 'zero-point' motion
Atoms always vibrate as long as they exist
Atoms keep moving due to cosmic background radiation

items.reveal_title: Zero-point energy — quantum residue at the bottom
items.reveal:
Every quantum oscillator has a ground-state energy of (1/2) h-bar omega above the bottom of its potential well. This isn't 'random' motion that can be removed — it's the lowest-energy state allowed by the uncertainty principle.

Helium remains liquid even at 0 K under normal pressure because zero-point motion is comparable to the inter-atomic binding energy — solidifying helium requires pressure to overcome it.

The third law of thermodynamics says you cannot reach 0 K in a finite number of steps: each cooling step removes a smaller and smaller fraction of remaining heat. Modern experiments have reached temperatures of around 100 picokelvin, but the laws of nature keep the last few degrees of headroom forever.
items.why: Absolute zero is imagined as 'no motion'. Quantum mechanics says even the ground state has motion — and you can never quite reach it anyway.

items.title: Earth's magnetic field is feeble — about 50 microtesla at the surface
items.claim: A typical fridge magnet generates a field of about 5 millitesla at its surface — about 100 times stronger than Earth's field. The field that swings every compass and protects life from solar wind is barely measurable with everyday instruments.
items.prompt: How does such a weak field deflect cosmic rays and the solar wind?

options.text: Charged particles are easily deflected by even weak fields when no other forces apply
Earth's field is much stronger than 50 microtesla in space
The deflection is from the atmosphere, not the magnetic field
The Sun's field cancels in the upper atmosphere

items.reveal_title: Lorentz force on a fast charged particle
items.reveal:
Earth's field at the surface is about 25-65 microtesla, depending on latitude. The field weakens with the cube of distance from the centre (it's nearly a magnetic dipole), so at the magnetopause (about 60,000 km out on the day side) it's down to a few nanotesla.

A proton in the solar wind has speed about 400 km/s. The Lorentz force qv × B is significant: gyroradius (the size of the circular path around a magnetic field line) is about 60 m for a typical solar wind proton near Earth — small compared with planetary scales. So charged particles spiral along field lines rather than crossing them.

The magnetosphere deflects the solar wind around Earth, funnels some particles to the poles (where they collide with the atmosphere and produce auroras), and traps high-energy particles in the Van Allen belts.
items.why: Earth's field 'feels' strong because it moves compasses noticeably. In tesla units it is millions of times weaker than an MRI scanner — but enough to deflect the solar wind.
